title: Rebuilding Credit After a Consumer Proposal
subtitle: Convert completion paperwork into a controlled credit re-entry

blocks.text: A consumer proposal can finish quietly. No bell rings, no confetti falls, and the credit bureaus do not gather for a synchronized update.

Completion is a legal milestone. Rebuilding is the organized work that follows. This course starts at the exit door. You will confirm whether your proposal is still active or fully performed, protect the proof, audit both reports and re-enter credit only when the cost and due dates fit your budget.
A completed proposal and an accurate credit report are linked, but they are not the same event. Keep your proof and check both bureau files.

You can leave your proposal knowing what is proven, what is fixed and what is still open.
blocks.detail: You will separate a finished proposal from a correct credit report, so no ad can sell you a reset you do not need.
blocks.extra: Chloe’s story comes next, then Zone 1 shows which side of completion you are on.

blocks.text: Meet Chloe
paragraphs: Chloe Sandhu is a pharmacy technician in Calgary with one proposal payment left. Next, she wants to replace her unreliable car with a loan that fits her life, not one that turns every commute into a luxury expedition.
A week before that last payment, an ad pops up online: “Instant credit reset! Vehicle approval, no questions asked!” Lots of exclamation marks. Almost no arithmetic.
The same week, her credit report shows a balance she thought the proposal had covered. Now she has two worries and one loud ad. She skips the ad and calls her Licensed Insolvency Trustee.
The trustee confirms her Certificate of Full Performance. Chloe puts it in one folder with the proposal, her payment record, her counselling confirmation and the trustee’s contact details.

Then she checks both reports. One bureau still shows the old balance, so she disputes it with proof and keeps the case number. Meanwhile, she builds a repair fund and compares one low-limit secured card.

Ten months later, her report is accurate and her recent payments are clean. The proposal did not vanish in a puff of administrative smoke. But when the first car offer arrives, Chloe says no and picks a cheaper car on a shorter term.
She still sees that ad now and then. It has not learned any arithmetic.

blocks.text: Chloe’s turning point was the order of her steps: confirm completion, fix the file, steady cash flow, then think about one useful account.
The conclusion
Her win was not a magic score. It was a confirmed exit, accurate records and a borrowing decision she could keep up.
Knowing which side of completion you are on tells you what to do next.
blocks.detail: You will confirm your status before you touch your credit file, so every correction request rests on proof.

sections.title: Zone 1: Know Which Side of Completion You Are On

blocks.text: A consumer proposal is a formal process under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, run by a Licensed Insolvency Trustee (LIT). It can last no more than five years. For the OSB process described here, eligible debts cannot be more than $250,000, not counting a mortgage on your main home.
If your proposal is still active

items.title: Follow the terms you filed. Keep your payment dates and finish any required duties. Ask the trustee before you change or speed up the plan.
Treat a missed payment as urgent. A monthly proposal is generally deemed annulled, which means cancelled, after three missed payments. Call the trustee early. Do not wait for the third surprise.
Send creditor calls to the trustee. If a creditor in your proposal contacts you, say you have a proposal and refer them to the trustee.
Pause new borrowing. A new account can add cost while the proposal is active. If you have a real need, talk to the trustee and check your budget first.

blocks.text: When fully performed

items.title: Confirm with the trustee that every required payment and duty is complete.
Get and keep your Certificate of Full Performance, issued through the proposal process.
Ask which creditors and government records get notice, and keep the trustee’s answer in your file.
Start the two-bureau audit. Do not expect every account to look the same on the same day.

blocks.text: Three missed monthly proposal payments can have serious consequences. An early call to the trustee is protection, not an admission of failure.

items.title: “I can fix an active proposal by negotiating separately with an included creditor.”
items.text: The trustee runs the proposal. Side deals can cause confusion and may clash with the filed process. Take the issue to the trustee.

sections.title: Zone 2: Build the Exit File, Then Check Both Reports

blocks.text: Keep copies in a secure folder. Hide account numbers before you share documents with anyone who does not need the full details.
Federal consumer guidance says both bureaus remove a consumer proposal three years after the included debts are paid off, or six years after signing, whichever comes first.

The rule does not promise identical wording, an instant update or a certain score. If a balance, date, creditor or status is wrong, use the bureau’s correction process and send copies of your proof. Involve the trustee if the proposal record itself is wrong.

items.title: Compare personal details, public-record sections, proposal details and every included account.
Circle only facts that are wrong: a bad balance, a bad status, a duplicate or an account you do not know. Also flag anything kept past the usual period.
Write one clear request for each issue. Say what is wrong, what the right fact is and which paper proves it.
Track dates and case numbers. Check both reports again after the investigation or the normal reporting cycle.
“A dispute is a request to remove any information I dislike.”
items.text: A dispute is for information that is incomplete, out of date or wrong. Accurate information can stay for the usual period.

sections.title: Zone 3: Re-enter Credit in the Right Order

blocks.text: The safest account to rebuild with is usually the one you understand, can afford and will manage steadily. A “credit-building” label can still hide a fee list with the charm of a tax form.

items.title: DAYS 0–30 · STABILIZE
items.text: File your completion papers, protect rent and essential bills, build a small cash buffer and list every due date you have.

items.title: DAYS 31–90 · VERIFY
items.text: Review both reports, send focused disputes and confirm that no proposal-related collection calls are still unresolved.

items.title: MONTHS 4–6 · TEST ONE TOOL
items.text: If your budget is steady, compare one secured card or other low-cost account. Check the deposit protection, fees, interest, grace period, limit and reporting.

items.title: MONTHS 7–12 · REPEAT
items.text: Pay every required amount on time and keep balances low. Skip unneeded applications and check statements for errors.

items.title: BEFORE A MAJOR LOAN · COMPARE
items.text: Compare the annual percentage rate, term, total cost of borrowing, add-ons and early-payment rules. Ask whether the payment still fits after a bad month.

blocks.text: A secured-card deposit is collateral, not a monthly payment. You still have to pay the card bill on time.

items.title: “Carrying a card balance and paying interest rebuilds faster.”
items.text: Interest is a cost. You do not need it to build a record. Small reported use and on-time payments can show activity without carrying debt on purpose.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Your last proposal payment cleared yesterday. What should you confirm before you apply for credit?
items.detail: Confirm with your LIT that every payment and duty is complete, and get the Certificate of Full Performance.

items.title: One report shows an included creditor with the wrong balance. What is the best next move?
items.detail: Use the bureau’s correction process. Send the report entry and copies of your completion and account proof.

items.title: A secured card has high fees and the payment would be tight. Does the label make it suitable?
items.detail: No. A credit-building label does not make unaffordable fees or tight cash flow safe.

items.title: Why review both Equifax and TransUnion reports?
items.detail: They keep separate files and may show or update proposal information differently.

items.title: Which five costs or terms should you compare before a major loan?
items.detail: APR, term, total cost of borrowing, add-ons and early-payment rules, plus whether you can afford it in a bad month.

sections.title: Your Action: Build Your Proposal Exit Dashboard

blocks.text: Use this after you speak with your LIT. Write facts, dates and next steps. Do not put full account numbers on a workbook you may carry or share.
A dashboard turns “I think it updated” into dates, papers, case numbers and decisions you can check.
Finish first. Prove it. Audit the records.
blocks.detail: Re-enter only with credit that solves a real need and fits a realistic budget. No responsible lender, bureau or educator can promise a higher score or an approval date.

items.title: Consumer proposal
items.text: A formal legal deal, run by a Licensed Insolvency Trustee, that offers creditors part or all of your unsecured debt back over time.

items.title: Licensed Insolvency Trustee (LIT)
items.text: A federally regulated professional who can run consumer proposals and bankruptcies.

items.title: Certificate of Full Performance
items.text: The certificate you get when the terms and required duties of a consumer proposal are done.

items.title: Fully performed
items.text: Every payment and duty in the accepted proposal has been completed.

items.title: Deemed annulment
items.text: Automatic cancellation of a proposal under the law when missed payments reach a set level.

items.title: Credit tradeline
items.text: One account entry on a credit report.

items.title: Annual percentage rate (APR)
items.text: The yearly cost of borrowing, shown in a standard way so you can compare credit offers.

questions: What does your trustee say your proposal status is, and as of what date?
Which completion papers do you have, and which are you still waiting on?
What does each credit report show for the proposal and your included accounts?
What is the wrong fact, what proves it, and what is the case number?
If you are thinking about a new account, what is it for, and what are the fee, the limit and the due date?
When will you check your reports again at 30, 90 and 365 days, and what habit will you repeat?
